title: The axe in the mouth
hookLine: a person is born with an axe in the mouth and cuts himself with bad speech

cards: Three days ago you heard the four marks of good speech. Today the Sutta Nipata shows the other side, with a story. A monk named Kokaliya comes to the Buddha with a complaint about two other monks.
Not just any two: Sariputta and Moggallana, the Buddha's two chief disciples. They have bad intentions, Kokaliya says. The Buddha answers him three times with the same words.
What happens next is hard to hear.

teach.b: Don't say that, Kokaliya, the Buddha tells him. Have confidence in Sariputta and Moggallana; they are good.
Kokaliya repeats the charge. The Buddha repeats the answer. A third time, the same.
Kokaliya gets up and leaves. Then, the text says, his body breaks out in boils, small as mustard seeds at first, growing larger and larger until they burst, and he dies.

The text says he is reborn in the hell called Paduma, and describes its torments at length, in the vivid, frightening terms the early texts use for the results of harmful acts. The lesson is in the verses.
A person is born, they say, with an axe in the mouth, and the fool cuts himself with it when he speaks badly. Look where the blade lands. Not on Sariputta and Moggallana.
Whoever praises someone who deserves blame, or blames someone who deserves praise, gathers bad luck with his own mouth. A loss at dice, the verses say, is small next to this.
And notice what the Buddha did. He didn't argue. He didn't punish.
He said the true thing, kindly, three times, and left the choice with Kokaliya.

how: Buddhist teachers often quote the axe-in-the-mouth verse when teaching right speech, and lay Buddhists who keep the five precepts include one against false speech.

o: an axe, for words that cut the speaker
a sharp tongue that wins every argument
a weapon used by the Buddha's enemies

games.q: the axe in the mouth: tap the pairs.
p: born in the mouth, cuts the speaker

s: the Buddha argued with Kokaliya until he gave in
he gave the same short answer three times, and Kokaliya left.
in the verse, the axe cuts the one who speaks
the fool cuts himself with it when he speaks badly.
blaming someone who deserves praise is called a fault too
the verses name both: praising the blameworthy and blaming the praiseworthy.

games.q: you're the Buddha. a monk accuses your two most trusted disciples of bad intentions. what do you do?
o: expel the monk on the spot.
say, three times, don't say that; they are good.
call the two disciples to defend themselves.
games.why: he simply repeats the true thing, kindly, three times. the monk walks out, and the rest of the story follows from his own words.

practice: Rest with your lips closed and your tongue soft, and feel how quiet it is when the axe is still. Bring to mind one person you're tempted to complain about, notice the sentence that's ready to go, and see who it would cut first.
Then let it rest, unspoken, and come back to the breath at the lips.

wordCard.voice: Kuthari, an axe. In the Kokaliya Sutta, the image for harmful speech: a blade a person is born with, which cuts the speaker first.

orig.note: Pali kuthari: an axe or hatchet, the blade born in the mouth in Sn 3.10.

carryVoice: Your line: let one word stay home. Some words do the most good unsaid. Day six hundred five.
